The Master said of Tsze-ch'an that he had four marks of the cultivated man: in his own bearing he was humble; in serving those above him, respectful; in providing for the people, kind; in directing the people, just.
The Master said: Yen P'ing knew how to keep a friendship. However long he had known a man, he showed him the same respect as at first.
The Master said: Tsang Wan housed his great tortoise in a hall with mountains carved on the pillar-tops and waterweed painted on the beams. What sort of wisdom was that?

Tsze-chang asked: The minister Tsze-wan took office three times and showed no joy, and three times was dismissed and showed no resentment; each time he handed the old government over fully to his successor. What do you make of him? The Master said: He was loyal. Was he humane? The Master said: I do not know — how does that make him humane? Tsze-chang went on: When Ts'ui killed the prince of Ch'i, Ch'an Wan, who owned forty horses, abandoned them and left the country. Coming to another state, he said, "They are no better here than our own officer Ts'ui," and left. He came to a second state, said the same, and left again. What do you make of him? The Master said: He was clean. Was he humane? The Master said: I do not know — how does that make him humane?
Chi Wan thought three times before he acted. The Master, hearing of it, said: Twice is enough.
The Master said: When the country was well governed, Ning Wu played the wise man; when it fell into disorder, he played the fool. His wisdom others may match — his folly they cannot.

When the Master was in Ch'an he said: Let me go home! Let me go home! The young ones of my school are headstrong and rash; they have made a fine, finished start, but do not know how to cut and shape themselves.
The Master said: Po-i and Shu-ch'i held no man's old wrongs against him, and so they were little resented.
The Master said: Who calls Wei-shang Kao straight? A man begged vinegar of him, and he begged it from a neighbor and gave it as his own.

The Master said: Smooth words, a fawning look, and overdone respect — Tso Ch'iu-ming was ashamed of them, and so am I. To hide a grudge against a man and act the friend to him — Tso Ch'iu-ming was ashamed of that, and so am I.

Yen Yuan and Chi Lu were at his side. The Master said: Why not each of you tell me what you long for? Tsze-lu said: I would have my carriage and horses and fine fur coats to share with my friends, and not mind if they wore them out. Yen Yuan said: I would not boast of my goodness or make a show of my labors. Tsze-lu said: And now we would hear the Master's longing. The Master said: To give the old their rest, to give friends my trust, and to cherish the young.
The Master said: It is hopeless! I have yet to meet the man who can see his own faults and arraign himself within.
The Master said: In a hamlet of ten households there is sure to be someone as loyal and true as I am — but none so fond of learning.

sections.label: Book VI
sections.title: On Disciples and the Humane Life

segments.text: The Master said: There is Yung — he could be seated facing south, like a prince. Chung-kung asked about Tsze-sang Po-tsze. The Master said: He will do; he does not fuss over small matters. Chung-kung said: To hold reverence within yourself and yet keep an easy hand in small matters when you govern the people — that may pass. But to be easy within and easy without as well — is that not too easy by far? The Master said: Yung is right.

Duke Ai asked which of the disciples loved learning. Confucius answered: There was Yen Hui; he loved to learn. He never turned his anger on the wrong person, and he never made the same mistake twice. Sadly, his life was cut short and he died; and now there is no one like him. I have not heard of anyone since who loves learning as he did.

When Tsze-hwa was sent on a mission to Ch'i, the disciple Zan asked for grain to provide for Tsze-hwa's mother. The Master said: Give her a fu. Zan asked for more. Give her an yu, said the Master. Zan gave her five ping. The Master said: When Ch'ih set out for Ch'i, he had sleek horses to his carriage and wore fine furs. I have heard that the cultivated person relieves the hard-pressed, but does not add to the riches of the rich.

When Yuan Sze was made governor of his town, the Master granted him nine hundred measures of grain, and Sze declined them. The Master said: Do not refuse. Could you not pass them on to the neighborhoods, the hamlets, and the villages around you?

Speaking of Chung-kung, the Master said: If the calf of a plowing ox is red-coated and well-horned, then even if men would rather not offer it, will the spirits of the mountains and rivers turn it away?
The Master said: Such was Hui — for three months together his heart would not stray from humaneness. The others may reach it for a day or a month, and no more.

Chi K'ang asked whether Chung-yu was fit to hold office. The Master said: Yu is decisive; what trouble would he have holding office? And is Ts'ze fit to hold office? The Master said: Ts'ze sees into things; what trouble would he have holding office? And Ch'iu? The Master said: Ch'iu has many talents; what trouble would he have holding office?

The head of the Chi family sent to make Min Tsze-ch'ien governor of Pi. Min Tsze-ch'ien said: Make my excuses for me, gently. If anyone comes asking a second time, I shall have to cross the Wan and leave the country.

When Po-niu was ill, the Master went to ask after him. He took his hand through the window and said: He is lost — it is the will of Heaven, alas. That such a man should have such a sickness! That such a man should have such a sickness!

The Master said: What a fine character Hui had! A bowl of rice, a gourd of water, a poor man's lane to live in — others could not have borne such misery, yet it never spoiled Hui's joy. What a fine character Hui had!

Yen Ch'iu said: It is not that I take no delight in your Way; my strength is not enough for it. The Master said: Those whose strength is not enough give out halfway along the road. You are drawing your own line before you start.
The Master said to Tsze-hsia: Be a scholar in the manner of the cultivated person, not in the manner of the small man.

When Tsze-yu was governor of Wu-ch'ang, the Master asked: Have you found any good men there? He answered: There is Tan-t'ai Mieh-ming. He never takes a shortcut when he walks, and he never comes to my office except on public business.

The Master said: Mang Chih-fan never boasts of what he does. When the army was in flight he brought up the rear, and as they reached the gate he whipped his horse forward and said: It was not that I dared to come last — my horse would not go any faster.
The Master said: Without the smooth tongue of the priest T'o and the good looks of Prince Chao of Sung, it is hard to get through these times unscathed.
The Master said: Who can go out except by the door? Why, then, will no one walk by this Way?

The Master said: Where the raw stuff outweighs the polish, a man is coarse; where the polish outweighs the raw stuff, he is a mere clerk. Raw stuff and polish in even measure — there you have the cultivated person.
The Master said: A man is born for uprightness. If a man loses it and lives on, he has only luck to thank that he is not dead.
The Master said: Those who know it are not equal to those who love it; and those who love it are not equal to those who delight in it.
The Master said: To those above the common run you may speak of the highest things; to those below it you may not.

Fan Ch'ih asked what wisdom is. The Master said: To give yourself wholly to the duties owed to other people, and to honor the spirits while keeping your distance from them — that may be called wisdom. He asked about humaneness. The Master said: The humane person takes on the hard part first and lets the reward come after — that may be called humaneness.
The Master said: The wise delight in water; the humane delight in mountains. The wise are active; the humane are still. The wise find joy; the humane find length of days.
The Master said: Ch'i, with one change, would rise to the level of Lu; and Lu, with one change, would rise to the level of the Way.
The Master said: A drinking-cup that is no longer a cup — what a cup! What a cup!

Tsai Wo asked: Suppose a humane man were told there was someone down a well — would he go in after him? The Master said: Why would he do that? You may send the cultivated person to the well, but you cannot make him jump in; you may deceive him, but you cannot make a fool of him.
The Master said: The cultivated person studies widely in all learning, and reins himself in with ritual; so he too can keep from overstepping what is right.
When the Master had been to see Nan-tsze, Tsze-lu was displeased. The Master swore an oath: If I have done anything wrong, may Heaven cast me off! May Heaven cast me off!
The Master said: The virtue of the Constant Mean — how perfect it is! And how long it has been rare among the people.

Tsze-kung said: Suppose a man who showered benefits on the people and could bring help to all — what would you say of him? Could he be called humane? The Master said: Why stop at humane? Surely he would be a sage. Even Yao and Shun fell short of that. As for the humane person: wishing to stand on his own feet, he helps others to stand; wishing to reach his goal, he helps others to reach theirs. To take what is near at hand — yourself — as the measure of others: that may be called the practice of humaneness.
The Master said: A transmitter and not a maker, trusting and loving the ancients — in this I venture to liken myself to our old P'ang.
The Master said: To store up knowledge in silence, to learn without ever tiring, to teach others without growing weary — which of these have I mastered?

The Master said: That I leave my character untended, that I fail to dig deep into what I learn, that I hear what is right and cannot move toward it, that I see my faults and cannot mend them — these are the things that trouble me.
When the Master was at his ease, his manner was relaxed and his face content.
The Master said: How far I have declined! It is a long time now since I dreamed, as I used to, of the duke of Chau.
The Master said: Set your heart on the Way. Hold fast to virtue. Lean on humaneness. And find your recreation in the arts.
The Master said: From the man who brought no more than a bundle of dried meat for my teaching, I have never withheld instruction.

The Master said: I do not open the way for one who is not burning to understand, nor help out one who is not struggling to put his thought into words. When I have shown a man one corner and he cannot come back to me with the other three, I do not go on.
When the Master ate beside someone in mourning, he never ate his fill. On a day he had wept, he did not sing.

The Master said to Yen Yuan: To take up office when you are called, and to retire quietly when you are not — only you and I can do this. Tsze-lu said: If you had charge of the armies of a great state, whom would you take with you? The Master said: Not the man who would fight a tiger bare-handed or wade a river with no boat, and die without a second thought. The one I want is the one who comes to the work wary, who loves to lay his plans, and so brings them off.
The Master said: If riches could be had for the seeking, I would seek them, even with whip in hand as a groom. But since they cannot, I will follow what I love.
The things the Master treated with the most care were fasting, war, and sickness.
When the Master was in Ch'i, he heard the Shao music, and for three months did not notice the taste of meat. He said: I never imagined that music could reach such heights.

Yen Yu said: Is the Master for the ruler of Wei? Tsze-kung said: I will go and ask him. He went in and said: What sort of men were Po-i and Shu-ch'i? The Master said: They were worthy men of old. And did they nurse any regret? The Master said: They sought humaneness, and they found it — what was there to regret? Tsze-kung came out and said: The Master is not for him.
The Master said: With coarse rice to eat, water to drink, and my bent arm for a pillow — even so I have joy. Riches and honor gotten by wrong are to me a passing cloud.
The Master said: Give me a few more years — fifty for the study of the Yi — and I might come through without grave faults.
The Master often spoke of the Odes, the History, and the keeping of ritual. On these he spoke often.

The Duke of Sheh asked Tsze-lu about Confucius, and Tsze-lu gave him no answer. The Master said: Why did you not simply tell him — here is a man who in his hunger for knowledge forgets to eat, who in his joy forgets his cares, and does not notice old age coming on?
The Master said: I am not one who was born knowing. I love the ancients, and I work hard to seek it there.
The Master did not talk of marvels, of feats of strength, of disorder, or of spirits.
The Master said: Walking with two others, I am sure of a teacher in them. I pick out what is good in them and follow it; what is bad, and mend it in myself.
The Master said: Heaven planted the virtue that is in me. Hwan T'ui — what can he do to me?
The Master said: Do you think, my friends, that I keep anything back? I keep nothing back from you. There is nothing I do that I do not share with you — that is my way.
The Master taught four things: letters, conduct, faithfulness, and good faith.

The Master said: A sage I cannot hope to see; if I could see a person of real worth, that would be enough. The Master said: A good man I cannot hope to see; if I could see a man of constancy, that would be enough. To have nothing and act as if you had, to be empty and act as if you were full, to be in want and act as if you were at ease — it is hard for such a man to have constancy.
The Master fished, but not with a net. He shot, but not at roosting birds.

The Master said: There may be those who act without knowing why; I am not one of them. To hear much, pick out the good, and follow it; to see much and hold it in mind — this is the next best thing to knowing.

The people of Hu-hsiang were hard to talk with, and when a boy from there was received by the Master, the disciples were uneasy. The Master said: I take a man as he comes to me; I do not answer for what he does once he leaves. Why be so harsh? When a man cleanses himself to come to me, I welcome the man he now is; I do not vouch for his past.
The Master said: Is humaneness so far off? I want to be humane, and there — humaneness is here.

The minister of crime of Ch'an asked whether Duke Chao knew ritual. Confucius said: He knew ritual. When Confucius had gone, the minister beckoned Wu-ma Ch'i forward and said: I had heard that the cultivated person takes no sides. Can he too take sides? The prince married a woman of the house of Wu, of his own surname, and called her "the elder Tsze of Wu." If this prince knew ritual, who does not? Wu-ma Ch'i reported this. The Master said: I am a lucky man. If I make a mistake, others are sure to know it.
When the Master was with someone who was singing and sang well, he would have him sing it again, and then join in.
The Master said: In letters I am perhaps no worse than other men. But to live out in my own conduct what the cultivated person professes — that I have not yet reached.

The Master said: A sage, or a man of perfect humaneness — how could I dare claim to be either? But that I strive toward it without tiring, and teach others without weariness — that much may be said of me. Kung-hsi Hwa said: And that is just what we, your disciples, cannot learn to do.

The Master was gravely ill, and Tsze-lu asked leave to pray for him. The Master said: Is there such a thing? Tsze-lu said: There is. The Eulogies say, "Prayer has been made for you to the spirits above and below." The Master said: Then my praying has been going on a long while.
The Master said: Extravagance breeds insolence, and stinginess breeds meanness. Better mean than insolent.
The Master said: The cultivated person is calm and at ease; the small man is always anxious and on edge.
The Master was gentle, yet firm; commanding, yet not harsh; respectful, yet at ease.

sections.label: Book VIII
sections.title: T'ai-po, and the Burden of the Scholar

segments.text: The Master said: T'ai-po may be said to have reached the very height of virtue. Three times he gave up the empire, and so quietly that the people never even knew enough to praise him.

The Master said: Respectfulness without ritual becomes wearisome fuss; caution without ritual becomes timidity; boldness without ritual becomes rebellion; plain speaking without ritual becomes rudeness. When those in high place are devoted to their own kin, the people are stirred to humaneness; when they do not forget their old friends, the people are kept from meanness.

Master Tsang was gravely ill, and called his disciples to him and said: Uncover my feet, uncover my hands. The Book of Poetry says, "In fear and trembling, as on the brink of a deep gulf, as treading thin ice." But now, my little children, I know that I have come through, my body whole.

Master Tsang was ill, and Meng Chang came to ask after him. Master Tsang said to him: When a bird is about to die, its cry is mournful; when a man is about to die, his words are good. There are three things the man of high rank should hold most important: that in his bearing and manner he keep clear of violence and carelessness; that in his looks he stay close to sincerity; and that in his words and tone he keep far from coarseness and impropriety. As for the sacrificial vessels, there are officers to see to those.

Master Tsang said: Gifted, yet asking of those who were not; full of knowledge, yet asking of those who had little; having, yet as though he had not; full, yet counting himself empty; wronged, yet picking no quarrel — I once had a friend who lived like this.

Master Tsang said: Suppose a man you could trust with a young orphaned prince, and charge with the rule of a domain of a hundred li, and whom no crisis, however great, could shake from his principles — is such a man a cultivated person? A cultivated person indeed.

Master Tsang said: The scholar cannot be without breadth of mind and tough endurance, for his burden is heavy and his road is long. Humaneness is the burden he takes as his own — is it not heavy? Only with death does the road end — is it not long?
The Master said: Roused by the Odes; established by ritual; perfected by music.
The Master said: The people may be made to follow a path, but not to understand it.
The Master said: A man who loves daring and chafes at poverty will turn to rebellion; and a man who is without humaneness, if you push your dislike of him too far, will turn to it as well.
The Master said: Though a man had gifts as splendid as the Duke of Chau's, if he were proud and stingy the rest would not be worth a glance.
The Master said: It is not easy to find a man who can study three years without his mind turning to a salary.

The Master said: Hold fast to sincerity, love learning, and guard the good way to the death. Do not enter a tottering state, nor stay in one in disorder. When the way prevails in the world, show yourself; when it does not, keep hidden. When a country is well governed, poverty and obscurity are a disgrace; when a country is badly governed, wealth and rank are a disgrace.
The Master said: If you do not hold the office, do not meddle in its business.
The Master said: When the music-master Chih began, and the close of the Kwan Tsu came — how it filled the ears!
The Master said: Ardent but not upright; ignorant but not careful; simple but not honest — such people are beyond me.
The Master said: Study as though you could never catch up, and as though you feared to lose what you had.
The Master said: How lofty was the way Shun and Yü held the empire — as if it were nothing to them!

The Master said: Great indeed was Yao as a ruler! How lofty! Heaven alone is grand, and Yao alone matched it. So vast was his virtue that the people could find no name for it. How lofty in all he accomplished, how brilliant in the forms and laws he set up!

Shun had five ministers, and the empire was well governed. King Wu said, "I have ten able ministers." Confucius said: How true the saying, that talent is hard to find! Only at the meeting of the houses of T'ang and Yü was it more abundant than in this age of Chau — and even then there was a woman among them, so the able men were no more than nine. King Wan held two parts of the empire in three, and with them still served the house of Yin. The virtue of the house of Chau may be called the very height of virtue.

The Master said: In Yü I can find no flaw. His own food and drink were poor, yet he was lavish in devotion to the spirits. His everyday clothes were plain, yet his sacrificial cap and apron were of the finest. He lived in a mean low house, yet poured out all his strength on the ditches and channels. In Yü I can find no flaw.
The Master rarely spoke of profit, or of fate, or of humaneness.

A man of the village of Ta-hsiang said: How great is K'ung! His learning is vast, yet there is no one thing that has made his name. The Master heard of it and said to his disciples: What, then, should I take up? Should I take up charioteering, or archery? Let me take up charioteering.

The Master said: The linen cap is what ritual prescribes; but nowadays men wear silk, which is cheaper, and in this I follow the common practice. Ritual prescribes bowing below the hall; but nowadays men bow only after they have gone up, which is arrogant. Here I keep to the old way and bow below the hall, even against the common practice.
There were four things the Master had wholly put away: he formed no foregone conclusions, laid down no rigid rules, was never obstinate, and was never self-centered.

When the Master was held in fear at K'wang, he said: King Wan is dead, but is not the cause of culture lodged here in me? Had Heaven meant this culture to perish, it would not have placed it in the hands of one born after him. And since Heaven does not mean it to perish, what can the men of K'wang do to me?

A high officer asked Tsze-kung: Surely your Master is a sage? How many things he can do! Tsze-kung said: Heaven has indeed set him on the way to sagehood, and given him many gifts besides. When the Master heard of it he said: Does the high officer know me? When I was young I was of low station, and so I learned many humble skills. But must the cultivated person be a man of many skills? No, he need not be. And Lao said: The Master used to say, "It was because I held no office that I picked up so many arts."
The Master said: Do I have knowledge? I have none. But when some plain man with an empty mind puts a question to me, I tap it at both ends, and search it out to the last.
The Master said: The phoenix does not come; the river gives up no chart. It is all over with me.

When the Master saw anyone in mourning dress, or in the cap and robes of full ceremony, or anyone who was blind, then even if they were younger than he, he would rise; and if he had to pass them, he passed quickly.

Yen Yuan, sighing, said: The more I look up to it, the higher it goes; the harder I bore into it, the firmer it grows. I see it ahead of me, and of a sudden it is behind. Step by step the Master leads us on with skill. He broadened me with culture and reined me in with ritual. When I would give it up, I cannot; and after I have spent all my strength, there it stands, sheer above me — yet for all my wish to follow, I find no way to reach it.

The Master was gravely ill, and Tsze-lu had the disciples act as if they were the household officers of a great man. In a lull in the illness the Master said: Long has Yu kept up this pretense! To make believe I have officers when I have none — whom would I be deceiving? Would I deceive Heaven? And better that I die in the hands of you, my disciples, than in the hands of officers. Even if I get no grand funeral, am I going to die by the roadside?
Tsze-kung said: Here is a fine gem. Shall I shut it in a case and keep it, or look for a good price and sell it? The Master said: Sell it! Sell it! But I would wait for the right price.

The Master wished to go and live among the nine wild tribes of the east. Someone said: They are rude. How could you? The Master said: If a cultivated person lived among them, what rudeness would be left?
The Master said: It was after I came back from Wei to Lu that the music was set right, and the Court hymns and the hymns of praise each found their proper place.

The Master said: To serve the high ministers and nobles abroad, and at home to serve my father and elder brothers; to do all that is owed to the dead, sparing no effort; and never to be mastered by wine — which of these have I managed?
Standing by a river, the Master said: It flows on like this, never stopping, day or night.
The Master said: I have never seen a man who loved virtue as he loves a beautiful face.

The Master said: It is like raising a mound. If I stop one basket short of finishing, I have stopped, and the stopping is mine. It is like leveling ground. Though I have thrown down but one basket, if I go forward, the going forward is mine.
The Master said: The one who never flagged when I set something before him — that was Hui.
The Master said of Yen Yuan: Alas! I watched him always going forward; I never once saw him stop.
The Master said: There are shoots that never come to flower, and there are flowers that never come to fruit.

The Master said: The young are to be held in awe. How do we know that those coming after will not match the men of today? But if a man reaches forty or fifty and has made no name, then there is nothing in him to hold in awe.

The Master said: Words of stern reproof — can a man help but assent to them? But it is the mending of his ways that matters. Words of gentle counsel — can a man help but be pleased with them? But it is the working out of their drift that matters. With a man who is pleased and never works it out, who assents and never mends his ways, I can do nothing at all.
The Master said: Hold faithfulness and sincerity above all. Take no friend who is not your equal in this. And when you are wrong, do not be afraid to set it right.
The Master said: You may carry off the commander of a great army, but you cannot carry off the will of even a common man.

The Master said: Standing in a tattered hemp-quilted coat beside men dressed in furs, and not ashamed — that is Yu. "He grudges nothing, he covets nothing; how can he do anything but good?" Tsze-lu took to reciting these lines over and over, until the Master said: This much is hardly enough to make a man good.
The Master said: Only when the year turns cold do we see that the pine and the cypress are the last to lose their leaves.
The Master said: The wise are free of doubt, the humane free of anxiety, the bold free of fear.

The Master said: There are men you can study beside who cannot go with you toward the Way; men who can go toward the Way with you, yet cannot stand firm in it beside you; men who can stand firm beside you, yet cannot weigh the changing case beside you.

"The blossoms of the wild cherry — how they flutter and turn! It is not that I do not think of you; it is that your house is so far away." The Master said: He did not really think of her. Had he, what distance could there be?
In his own village, the Master was plain and sincere, and seemed almost unable to speak. But in the ancestral temple and at court, he spoke readily and to the point of every matter, only with care.

Waiting at court, when he spoke with the officers of lower rank he was free and frank; with those of higher rank he was warm and yet exact. When the ruler was present, his manner showed a respectful unease, grave and yet composed.

When the prince called on him to receive a guest, his face would change and his legs seemed to move with difficulty. He bowed to the officers on either side of him, swinging his arm left or right as their place required, and kept the skirts of his robe hanging even before and behind. He hurried forward, his arms spread like the wings of a bird. When the guest had gone, he always brought back word to the prince: "The visitor is no longer looking back."

Entering the palace gate, he bent his body as though the gate were too low to let him through. He did not stand in the middle of the gateway, and going in or out he did not tread on the threshold. Passing the prince's empty place, his face would change, his legs seemed to fail him, and his words came as though he had hardly breath to speak them. He went up to the hall holding the hem of his robe in both hands, his body bent, his breath held as though he dared not breathe. Coming out, after he had gone down one step his face relaxed and grew content; at the foot of the steps he went quickly forward, his arms spread like wings, and once back in his place his manner still showed a respectful unease.

Carrying the prince's tablet of office, he bent as if its weight were too much for him. He held it no higher than the hands held in bowing, and no lower than the hands held in offering a gift; his face changed and looked apprehensive, and he dragged his feet as though something held them to the ground. When he laid out the gifts he had been charged with, his look was calm; at the private audience that followed, his look was glad.

The Master did not use deep purple or puce in the trim of his clothes, and even at home he wore nothing red or reddish. In warm weather he wore a single garment of fine or coarse cloth, but always over an inner one. Over lamb's fur he wore black, over fawn's fur white, over fox's fur yellow. His everyday fur robe was long, with the right sleeve cut short. His nightgown he had made half again as long as his body. At home he sat on thick furs of fox or badger. When his mourning was over, there was nothing he did not hang from his girdle. His skirt, except where it had to be of the full curtain cut, was narrow at the top and wide below. He did not wear lamb's fur or a black cap when paying a visit of condolence. On the first day of the month he put on his court robes and presented himself at court.
When fasting, he made sure his clothes were bright and clean and of linen. When fasting, he changed his food, and changed the place where he usually sat.

He did not mind his rice being finely cleaned, nor his meat finely minced. He would not eat rice that had gone sour from heat or damp, nor fish or flesh that had turned. He would not eat what had lost its color, nor what smelled bad, nor what was badly cooked, nor what was out of season. He would not eat meat that was not cut square, nor anything served without its proper sauce. Though there was meat in plenty, he did not let it outweigh the rice. Only with wine did he set himself no limit — but he never drank to confusion. Wine and dried meat from the market he would not touch. He was never without ginger when he ate. He did not eat much. After serving at the prince's sacrifice, he did not keep the meat overnight; the meat of his own family's sacrifice he did not keep past three days, for after three days it could not be eaten. At his meals he did not talk; in his bed he did not speak. Though his meal were only coarse rice and vegetable broth, he would set a little aside as an offering, with a grave and reverent air.
If his mat was not straight, he would not sit on it.

When the men of his village drank together, he did not leave until the elders with their staffs had gone out. When the villagers held the rite to drive off evil spirits, he put on his court robes and stood on the eastern steps.

When he was sending his respects to someone in another state, he bowed twice as he saw the messenger off. When Chi K'ang sent him a present of medicine, he bowed and received it, but said: "I do not know this drug; I dare not taste it."
The stable burned down. On returning from court the Master said, "Was anyone hurt?" He did not ask about the horses.

When the prince sent him a gift of cooked meat, he would straighten his mat, taste it first, and then share it out. When the prince sent him uncooked meat, he had it cooked and offered it to his ancestors. When the prince sent him a living animal, he kept it alive. Attending the prince at a meal, while the prince made the offering he tasted everything first. When he was ill and the prince came to see him, he had his head laid to the east, his court robes spread over him, and his sash drawn across them. When the prince's summons came, he set out at once, without waiting for the horses to be yoked.
When he entered the ancestral temple of the state, he asked about everything.

When a friend died and there was no kinsman to see to the rites, he would say, "It is mine to bury him." When a friend sent him a gift, even a carriage and horses, he did not bow for it; the only gift he bowed for was meat from a sacrifice.

In bed he did not lie like a corpse. At home he put on no formal air. When he saw anyone in mourning, even an acquaintance, his face would change; when he saw anyone wearing the cap of office, or a blind man, even one he knew well, he would greet him with full ceremony. To a man in mourning he bowed forward over the crossbar of his carriage, and he bowed the same way to anyone carrying the census tables. At a feast where the table was laid with abundance, his face would change and he would rise. At a sudden clap of thunder or a fierce wind, his face would change.
About to mount his carriage, he stood straight and took hold of the cord. In the carriage he did not turn his head right round, did not speak in haste, and did not point with his hand.

Startled, the bird rises, circles, and only then settles. The Master said, "There is the hen-pheasant on the mountain bridge — she knows her season, she knows her season!" Tsze-lu made a gesture toward her; she sniffed three times and rose.

sections.label: Book XI
sections.title: The Disciples, and the Death of Hui

segments.text: The Master said: In ceremony and music, the men of old were called rough countrymen, while the men of these later days are called polished gentlemen. But if I had to choose how to use them, I would follow the men of old.

The Master said: Of those who were with me in Ch'an and Ts'ai, not one is left to come to my door. For their virtue and conduct there were Yen Yuan, Min Tsze-ch'ien, Zan Po-niu, and Chung-kung; for their gift of speech, Tsai Wo and Tsze-kung; for skill in government, Zan Yu and Chi Lu; for learning, Tsze-yu and Tsze-hsia.
The Master said: Hui is no help to me. There is nothing I say that does not delight him.
The Master said: What a devoted son Min Tsze-ch'ien is! No one ever finds fault with what his own parents and brothers say in his praise.
Nan Yung kept repeating the verse about the white scepter-stone. Confucius gave him his elder brother's daughter in marriage.

Chi K'ang asked which of the disciples loved learning. Confucius answered: There was Yen Hui; he loved learning. Sadly, his life was cut short and he died; and now there is no one who loves learning as he did.

When Yen Yuan died, his father Yen Lu begged for the Master's carriage, to sell it and buy an outer shell for the coffin. The Master said: Gifted or not, a man still calls his son his son. When my own son Li died, he had a coffin but no outer shell. I did not go on foot to get him one, for having ranked among the great officers, it was not proper for me to walk.
When Yen Yuan died, the Master said: Alas! Heaven is destroying me! Heaven is destroying me!

When Yen Yuan died, the Master wept for him without restraint. His followers said: Master, your grief is too much. He said: Too much? If I am not to mourn bitterly for this man, then for whom should I mourn?

When Yen Yuan died, the disciples wanted to give him a grand funeral. The Master said: You must not. They gave him a grand funeral all the same. The Master said: Hui treated me as a father; I have not been able to treat him as a son. The fault is not mine — it is yours, my disciples.

Chi Lu asked how to serve the spirits of the dead. The Master said: You cannot yet serve the living — how can you serve the dead? Chi Lu said: May I ask about death? The Master said: You do not yet know life — how can you know death?
Min was standing at the Master's side, mild and upright; Tsze-lu, bold and soldierly; Zan Yu and Tsze-kung, easy and frank. The Master was pleased. But he said: A man like Yu will not die in his bed.

Some men of Lu were going to pull down the Long Treasury and build it anew. Min Tsze-ch'ien said: Why not leave it as it was? Why must it be torn down and remade? The Master said: This man rarely speaks, but when he does, he hits the mark.

The Master said: What is Yu's lute doing at my door? After this the other disciples lost their respect for Tsze-lu. The Master said: Yu has climbed to the hall, though he has not yet entered the inner rooms.

Tsze-kung asked which was the better, Shih or Shang. The Master said: Shih goes too far; Shang does not go far enough. Then Shih is the better? said Tsze-kung. The Master said: To go too far is as wrong as to fall short.

The head of the Chi family was richer than the Duke of Chau had ever been, and yet Ch'iu gathered his taxes for him and swelled his wealth still more. The Master said: He is no disciple of mine. Sound the drum, my little ones, and go after him.
Ch'ai is simple; Shan is dull; Shih puts on a fine front; Yu is coarse.
The Master said: Hui has nearly reached it — yet he is often in want. Ts'ze does not bow to the will of Heaven, and goes out and makes money; but his judgments are often right.
Tsze-chang asked what marks the good man. The Master said: He does not tread in the tracks of others; but neither has he entered the inner chamber of the sage.
The Master said: A man's talk may sound solid and sincere, but is he truly a cultivated person, or only grave in appearance?

Tsze-lu asked whether he should at once act on what he heard. The Master said: Your father and elder brothers are still alive — how can you act at once on what you hear? Zan Yu asked the same thing: should he at once act on what he heard? The Master said: Act on it at once. Kung-hsi Hwa said: When Yu asked whether to act at once, you spoke of his father and brothers; when Ch'iu asked the same, you told him to act at once. I am confused, and venture to ask why. The Master said: Ch'iu holds back, so I urged him forward. Yu has energy enough for two, so I reined him in.
When the Master was held in fear in K'wang, Yen Yuan fell behind. When he caught up, the Master said: I thought you were dead. Hui said: While you are alive, how would I dare to die?

Chi Tsze-zan asked whether Chung Yu and Zan Ch'iu could be called great ministers. The Master said: I thought you would ask about some remarkable men, and you only ask about Yu and Ch'iu. A great minister is one who serves his prince by what is right, and steps down when he cannot. As for Yu and Ch'iu, they may be called ordinary ministers. Then they would always follow their chief? said Tsze-zan. The Master said: In the killing of a father or a prince, they would not follow him.

Tsze-lu had Tsze-kao made governor of Pi. The Master said: You are ruining another man's son. Tsze-lu said: There are the people to govern, and the altars of the land and grain to tend. Why must a man read books before he can be said to have learned? The Master said: It is just this that makes me hate a glib tongue.

Tsze-lu, Tsang Hsi, Zan Yu, and Kung-hsi Hwa were sitting with the Master. He said: I am a little older than you, but never mind that. Day after day you say, "No one knows us." Well, if some ruler did know you, what would you wish to do? Tsze-lu answered quickly: Give me a state of a thousand chariots, hemmed in between great powers, overrun by armies and stricken with famine; let me govern it, and in three years I could make the people brave and teach them the path of right. The Master smiled at him. And you, Ch'iu — what would you wish? Ch'iu answered: Give me a district of sixty or seventy li, or fifty or sixty, and in three years I could bring the people plenty. As for ritual and music, I would wait for a finer man than I. And you, Ch'ih? Ch'ih answered: I do not say I am able, but I would like to learn. At the services in the ancestral temple, and when the princes meet the sovereign, I would like, in dark robe and black cap, to assist in some small way. And you, Tien — what would you wish? Tien, who had been softly playing the lute, let the last note fade, set it down, and rose. My wish, he said, is not like theirs. What harm in that? said the Master. Speak out, like the rest. Then Tien said: In the last month of spring, with the spring clothes all made, I would go with five or six grown men and six or seven boys to bathe in the Yi, take the breeze among the rain altars, and come home singing. The Master heaved a sigh and said: I am with Tien. When the other three had gone out, Tsang Hsi stayed behind and asked: What did you make of what the three of them said? The Master said: Each one simply told his wish. Then why did you smile at Yu? said Hsi. The Master said: A state is governed by ritual, and his words were not modest; that is why I smiled. But surely Ch'iu was not speaking of a state? The Master said: Where have you seen a district of sixty or seventy li, or fifty or sixty, that was not a state? And Ch'ih — was he not speaking of a state? The Master said: Ancestral temples, and the audiences of princes — whose business are these but a ruler's? If Ch'ih would only assist in some small way, who then could do the great?

Yen Yuan asked about humaneness. The Master said: To master yourself and return to ritual is humaneness. Let a man master himself and return to ritual for a single day, and the whole world would grant him humaneness. But this work is one's own; it does not come from others. Yen Yuan said: May I ask the steps of it? The Master said: Look at nothing contrary to ritual; listen to nothing contrary to ritual; say nothing contrary to ritual; do nothing contrary to ritual. Yen Yuan said: Slow as I am, I will make this my whole business.

Chung-kung asked about humaneness. The Master said: Out in the world, behave to everyone as if you were receiving a great guest; deal with the people as if you were assisting at a great sacrifice. What you do not want done to yourself, do not do to others. Then there will be no murmuring against you in the state, and none in your own house. Chung-kung said: Slow as I am, I will make this my whole business.

Sze-ma Niu asked about humaneness. The Master said: The humane man is slow and careful in his speech. Slow and careful in his speech! said Niu. Is that all humaneness means? The Master said: When a thing is hard to do, can a man be other than slow to speak of it?

Sze-ma Niu asked about the cultivated person. The Master said: The cultivated person knows neither worry nor fear. Without worry or fear! said Niu. Is that all it means to be a cultivated person? The Master said: When he looks within and finds nothing wrong, what has he to worry about, what has he to fear?

Sze-ma Niu, full of grief, said: Every other man has brothers; I alone have none. Tsze-hsia said to him: I have heard it said — death and life are decreed, riches and honor rest with Heaven. The cultivated person is reverent and lets nothing slip; he is courteous to others and keeps to ritual — and then all within the four seas are his brothers. Why should the cultivated person grieve that he has no brothers?

Tsze-chang asked what it is to see clearly. The Master said: The man on whom slander that soaks in drop by drop, and accusations that cut to the quick, can get no hold — he may be said to see clearly. The man on whom soaking slander and cutting accusations can get no hold — he may be said to see far.

Tsze-kung asked about government. The Master said: Enough food, enough weapons, and the people's trust in their ruler. Tsze-kung said: If you had no choice but to give up one of the three, which would you let go first? The weapons, said the Master. Tsze-kung said: If you had no choice but to give up one of the other two, which would you let go? Give up the food, said the Master. From of old, death has come to all men; but a people without trust in its rulers cannot stand at all.

Chi Tsze-ch'ang said: A cultivated person needs only the solid stuff in him; what use has he for polish? Tsze-kung said: A pity, sir, that you should speak so of the cultivated person — for not even a team of four horses can overtake the spoken word. Polish is no different from the stuff, and the stuff no different from the polish. Strip the hide of a tiger or a leopard of its hair, and it is no different from the hide of a dog or a goat.

Duke Ai asked Yu Zo: The year is lean and there is not enough to meet my needs — what should I do? Yu Zo answered: Why not simply take a tithe, one part in ten? With two parts in ten, said the duke, I still have not enough — how could I manage on one? Yu Zo answered: If the people have enough, how should their prince be left wanting? And if the people are in want, how can their prince have enough?

Tsze-chang asked how to build up virtue and to see through delusions. The Master said: Hold faithfulness and sincerity above all, and keep moving toward what is right — this is how virtue is built up. You love a man and want him to live; you hate him and want him to die. To want him alive and dead by turns — that is delusion. "Not for her wealth, but only because you have found someone new."

Duke Ching of Ch'i asked Confucius about government. Confucius answered: Let the ruler be ruler, the minister minister, the father father, and the son son. Good! said the duke. For truly, if the ruler is no ruler, the minister no minister, the father no father, and the son no son, then though I have my revenue, shall I ever get to enjoy it?
The Master said: To settle a lawsuit on half a word — that is Yu! Tsze-lu never slept on a promise.
The Master said: In hearing lawsuits I am no better than any other man. What is needed is to bring it about that there are no lawsuits at all.
Tsze-chang asked about government. The Master said: Keep its affairs always before your mind, and carry them out with a whole heart.
The Master said: Study widely in all learning, and rein yourself in with ritual — and you too can keep from overstepping what is right.
The Master said: The cultivated person helps others to what is good in them, and not to what is bad. The small man does the opposite.
Chi K'ang asked Confucius about government. Confucius answered: To govern is to set right. If you lead with what is right, who will dare not be right?
Chi K'ang, troubled by the number of thieves, asked Confucius what to do about them. Confucius answered: If you yourself were free of greed, the people would not steal though you paid them to.

Chi K'ang asked Confucius about government, saying: Suppose I put the lawless to death for the sake of the law-abiding — what of that? Confucius answered: You are here to govern; what need have you to kill at all? Set your own heart on what is good, and the people will be good. The virtue of the ruler is the wind, the virtue of the people the grass; when the wind blows across it, the grass must bend.

Tsze-chang asked: What must a man be to be called distinguished? The Master said: What do you mean by distinguished? Tsze-chang answered: To be heard of throughout the state, and heard of throughout his clan. The Master said: That is being known of, not being distinguished. The distinguished man is solid and straight, and loves what is right; he weighs men's words and reads their faces, and takes care to put himself below others. Such a man is sure to be distinguished in the state, and distinguished in his clan. But the man who is merely known of puts on the look of virtue while his deeds run against it, and never once doubts himself. He too is sure to be heard of in the state, and heard of in his clan.

Fan Ch'ih, walking with the Master below the rain altars, said: May I ask how to build up virtue, to clear away hidden faults, and to see through delusions? The Master said: A fine question! Put the work first and the reward after — is that not the way to build up virtue? Attack the wrong in yourself and not the wrong in others — is that not the way to clear away hidden faults? For a single morning's rage to forget yourself and bring ruin even on your parents — is that not delusion?

Fan Ch'ih asked about humaneness. The Master said: It is to love others. He asked about wisdom. The Master said: It is to know others. Fan Ch'ih did not yet understand. The Master said: Raise up the straight and set them over the crooked, and you can make the crooked straight. Fan Ch'ih withdrew, and seeing Tsze-hsia he said: A while ago I went to the Master and asked about wisdom, and he said, Raise up the straight and set them over the crooked, and you can make the crooked straight. What did he mean? Tsze-hsia said: Rich words indeed! When Shun ruled the world, he chose out from among the many and raised up Kao-yao, and all who lacked humaneness were gone. When T'ang ruled the world, he chose out from among the many and raised up I Yin, and all who lacked humaneness were gone.
Tsze-kung asked about friends. The Master said: Counsel them faithfully and lead them on with skill, but if they will not hear, then stop; do not bring disgrace on yourself.
Master Tsang said: The cultivated person gathers friends around him through his learning, and through his friends builds up his humaneness.
Tsze-lu asked about government. The Master said: Go before the people, and labor on their behalf. When Tsze-lu asked for more, he said: Never let it weary you.

Chung-kung, now chief minister to the head of the Chi family, asked about government. The Master said: Put your various officers to work first; pardon small faults; and raise men of worth and ability to office. Chung-kung said: How am I to know the men of worth and ability, so as to raise them? He was answered: Raise those you know. As for those you do not — will others let them slip by?

Tsze-lu said: The ruler of Wei is waiting for you to take a hand in his government. What would you put first? The Master said: What is needed is to set names right. So indeed! said Tsze-lu. You are wide of the mark. Why this setting names right? The Master said: How crude you are, Yu! On a matter he does not understand, the cultivated person holds back. If names are not right, speech does not fit the truth of things. If speech does not fit the truth of things, affairs cannot be carried through. If affairs cannot be carried through, ritual and music do not flourish. If ritual and music do not flourish, punishments miss their mark. And if punishments miss their mark, the people do not know where to put hand or foot. So the cultivated person uses only names that can be spoken truly, and says only what can be carried out. In his words, he allows nothing slipshod — that is all.

Fan Ch'ih asked to be taught farming. The Master said: For that you had better an old farmer than me. He asked to be taught gardening. The Master said: For that you had better an old gardener than me. When Fan Ch'ih had gone out, the Master said: A small man indeed, this Fan Hsu! If those above love ritual, the people will not dare to be irreverent. If those above love what is right, the people will not dare to disobey. If those above love good faith, the people will not dare to be false. Let it be so, and people from every quarter will come, their children strapped to their backs. What need has he of farming?

The Master said: A man may know the three hundred odes by heart, yet if he is given a charge in government and cannot manage it, or sent abroad on a mission and cannot answer for himself, then for all his learning, what use is it?
The Master said: When a ruler's own conduct is upright, things get done without his giving orders. When his own conduct is not upright, he may give orders, but they will not be obeyed.
The Master said: In their governments, Lu and Wei are brothers.

The Master said of Ching, a scion of the ducal house of Wei, that he managed a household well. When he first had a little, he said: Now it begins to come together. When it grew, he said: Now it is complete. When he was rich, he said: Now it is splendid.

When the Master went to Wei, Zan Yu drove his carriage. The Master remarked: What a crowd of people! Zan Yu said: Since they are so many, what more should be done for them? Enrich them, was the reply. And when they are enriched, what more? The Master said: Teach them.
The Master said: Were any ruler to employ me, in twelve months I should have made some headway, and in three years the work would be complete.
The Master said: "Let good men govern a country for a hundred years running, and they could master cruelty and do away with killing." How true that saying is!
The Master said: Even were a true king to arise, it would still take a generation before humaneness prevailed.
The Master said: If a man can set his own conduct right, what trouble will he have in government? If he cannot set himself right, what has he to do with setting others right?

When the disciple Zan came back from court, the Master said: Why so late? He answered: There was government business. The Master said: It must have been the family's affairs. Had there been government business, then though I hold no office now, I should have been consulted.

Duke Ting asked: Is there a single saying that can make a country flourish? Confucius answered: No saying can do quite that. But there is one that people have — "To be a prince is hard; to be a minister is not easy." If a ruler grasps how hard it is to be a prince, is that saying not close to making a country flourish? The duke said: Is there a single saying that can ruin a country? Confucius answered: No saying can do quite that. But there is one that people have — "I take no pleasure in being a prince, save that no one dares oppose what I say." Now if his words are good and no one opposes them, well and good. But if his words are bad and no one opposes them, is that saying not close to ruining a country?
The Duke of Sheh asked about government. The Master said: Good government is when those near at hand are made glad, and those far off are drawn to come.

Tsze-hsia, now governor of Chu-fu, asked about government. The Master said: Do not want things done quickly; do not look to small gains. Want things done quickly, and they will not be done well. Look to small gains, and great things will not be accomplished.

The Duke of Sheh told Confucius: Among us there is a man so upright that when his father stole a sheep, he bore witness against him. Confucius said: Among us the upright are otherwise. The father covers for the son, and the son covers for the father — and uprightness is to be found in that.
Fan Ch'ih asked about humaneness. The Master said: At home, be dignified; in your work, be careful; with others, be wholehearted. Even among the rude tribes you must not let these go.

Tsze-kung asked: What must a man be like to be called fit for office? The Master said: One who keeps a sense of shame in his own conduct, and who, sent anywhere on his ruler's business, does not disgrace it — he may be called fit. And next below him? One whom his kinsmen call good to his parents, and his neighbors call respectful to his elders. And the rank below that? One firm to keep his word and carry through what he sets out to do — a stubborn small man, perhaps, yet he may make the next rank. And what of those in government today? The Master said: Pah — vessels of a peck and a hamper, not worth the reckoning.

The Master said: Since I cannot find men who hold the middle way to share my teaching with, I must take the ardent and the wary. The ardent press forward and lay hold; the wary hold back from what is wrong.

The Master said: The men of the south have a saying — "A man without constancy cannot be a diviner or a healer." Well said! Of one inconstant in his virtue it is written, "He will be visited with disgrace." The Master said: Such a man simply does not read the signs.
The Master said: The cultivated person is in harmony but does not echo; the small man echoes but is not in harmony.

Tsze-kung asked: What of a man whom all his neighbors love? The Master said: That is not yet enough. And one whom all his neighbors hate? The Master said: That is not enough either. Better that the good among them love him, and the bad hate him.

The Master said: The cultivated person is easy to serve but hard to please. Try to please him by what is not right, and he is not pleased; but in setting men to work, he uses each according to what he can do. The small man is hard to serve but easy to please. Please him even by what is not right, and he is pleased; but in setting men to work, he asks everything of every one.
The Master said: The cultivated person has an easy dignity without pride; the small man has pride without an easy dignity.
The Master said: Firm, enduring, plain, slow to speak — these are near to humaneness.

Tsze-lu asked: What must a man be like to be called a scholar? The Master said: Earnest, pressing, yet cordial — that is the scholar. With his friends, earnest and pressing; with his brothers, cordial.
The Master said: Let a good man teach the people for seven years, and they may then be fit to bear arms.
The Master said: To send an untrained people to war is to throw them away.

Hsien asked what is shameful. The Master said: When good government prevails in a state, to think only of your salary; and when bad government prevails, still to think only of your salary — that is shameful.

When the love of mastery, boasting, resentment, and greed are all held down — may that be called humaneness? The Master said: That may be called doing what is hard. Whether it is humaneness, I do not know.
The Master said: A scholar who clings to his comforts is not fit to be called a scholar.
The Master said: When good government prevails in a state, speak boldly and act boldly. When bad government prevails, act boldly but speak with reserve.

The Master said: The humane are sure to have something to say, but those who have something to say are not always humane. Men of principle are sure to be bold, but the bold are not always men of principle.

Nan-kung Kwo put a question to Confucius: Yi was a master archer, and Ao could push a boat over dry land — yet neither died a natural death. Yu and Chi worked the soil with their own hands, and they came to possess the kingdom. The Master made no answer; but when Nan-kung Kwo had gone out, he said: A cultivated person, this man! A man who prizes virtue, this man!
The Master said: There have been cultivated people who fell short of humaneness — alas, yes. But there has never been a small man who possessed it.
The Master said: Can there be love that does not make you strict with the one you love? Can there be loyalty that does not make you teach the one you serve?

The Master said: In drawing up the state's proclamations, P'i Shan made the rough draft; Shi-shu went over it and weighed its contents; Tsze-yu, who managed foreign affairs, polished the wording; and Tsze-ch'an of Tung-li gave it grace and finish.

Someone asked about Tsze-ch'an. The Master said: A kind man. He asked about Tsze-hsi. The Master said: That man! That man! He asked about Kwan Chung. The Master said: This is a man who stripped the head of the Po family of the town of Pien with its three hundred households — and to the end of his days, eating only coarse rice, the man never spoke a word of complaint.
The Master said: To be poor and not complain is hard. To be rich and not proud is easy.
The Master said: Mang Kung-ch'o is more than fit to be steward to great houses like Chao and Wei, but he is not fit to be a minister in a small state like Tang or Hsieh.

Tsze-lu asked what makes a complete man. The Master said: Take the wisdom of Tsang Wu-chung, the freedom from greed of Kung-ch'o, the courage of Chwang of Pien, and the many talents of Zan Ch'iu, and round them off with ritual and music — such a one might be called a complete man. Then he added: But why must a complete man today be all of that? The man who, seeing a chance for gain, thinks of what is right; who, seeing danger, is ready to give his life; and who does not forget an old promise, however far back it was made — such a man too may be called complete.

The Master asked Kung-ming Chia about Kung-shu Wan, saying: Is it true that your master does not speak, does not laugh, and does not take? Kung-ming Chia replied: Whoever told you that went too far. My master speaks when it is time to speak, so men never tire of his speaking. He laughs when there is reason for joy, so men never tire of his laughing. He takes only when it is right to take, so men never tire of his taking. The Master said: Is that so? Can it really be so with him?
The Master said: Tsang Wu-chung, holding the town of Fang, pressed the Duke of Lu to name a successor to his family. They say he did not force his ruler in this — but I believe he did.
The Master said: Duke Wan of Tsin was crafty and not upright. Duke Hwan of Ch'i was upright and not crafty.

Tsze-lu said: When Duke Hwan had his brother Chiu killed, Shao Hu died with their master, but Kwan Chung did not die. May I not say he fell short of humaneness? The Master said: Duke Hwan brought all the princes together nine times, and not by force of chariots and arms — this was the work of Kwan Chung. Such was his humaneness! Such was his humaneness!

Tsze-kung said: Kwan Chung, I think, fell short of humaneness. When Duke Hwan had his brother Chiu killed, Kwan Chung could not bring himself to die with him — and more, he became Hwan's prime minister. The Master said: Kwan Chung served as Duke Hwan's prime minister, made him leader of all the princes, and set the whole kingdom right; to this day the people enjoy what he gave them. But for Kwan Chung, we would be wearing our hair loose and folding our coats to the left. Would you have him keep the petty good faith of common men and women, who hang themselves in a ditch and no one ever the wiser?
Hsien, the steward who had served Kung-shu Wan, went up to the prince's court at his master's side. When the Master heard of it, he said: He earned the name Wan — the accomplished.

The Master was speaking of the misrule of Duke Ling of Wei, when Ch'i K'ang said: If he is like that, how does he not lose his state? Confucius said: Chung-shu Yu has charge of his guests and strangers, the priest T'o has charge of his ancestral temple, and Wang-sun Chia has charge of the army. With officers like these, how would he lose his state?
The Master said: A man who makes his claims without modesty will find them hard to make good.

Chan Ch'ang murdered Duke Chien of Ch'i. Confucius bathed, went to court, and reported to Duke Ai: Chan Hang has slain his ruler. I beg you to punish him. The Duke said: Tell the chiefs of the three families. Confucius withdrew and said: Coming after the great officers, I did not dare to leave such a thing unreported — and my prince says, "Tell the three families." He went to the three families and reported it, and they would not act. Confucius said: Coming after the great officers, I did not dare to leave such a thing unreported.
Tsze-lu asked how to serve a ruler. The Master said: Do not deceive him — and do stand up to him to his face.
The Master said: The cultivated person makes his way upward; the small man makes his way downward.
The Master said: In old times men learned for their own sake; nowadays men learn to impress others.

Chu Po-yu sent a messenger with kind inquiries to Confucius. Confucius sat him down and asked: What is your master busy with? The messenger replied: My master longs to make his faults few, but he has not yet managed it. When the messenger had gone out, the Master said: A messenger indeed! A messenger indeed!
The Master said: A man who does not hold a given office should not meddle in its business.
Master Tsang said: The cultivated person, in his thoughts, does not stray beyond his place.
The Master said: The cultivated person is modest in his words and outdoes them in his deeds.

The Master said: The way of the cultivated person is threefold, and I fall short of all three: humane, he is free of anxiety; wise, he is free of confusion; brave, he is free of fear. Tsze-kung said: Master, that is your own portrait.
Tsze-kung was given to weighing other men against each other. The Master said: Ts'ze must have reached great heights! I myself have no time to spare for that.
The Master said: I will not worry that others do not know me; I will worry that I am not able.

The Master said: Not to guard beforehand against being deceived, nor to suspect beforehand that you will not be trusted, and yet to see these things coming the moment they appear — is that not the mark of a person of worth?

Wei-shang Mau said to Confucius: Ch'iu, why do you keep perching here and there like this? Are you not a smooth-tongued talker? Confucius said: I would not dare play the smooth talker — but I do hate stubbornness.
The Master said: A fine horse is praised not for its strength but for its character.
Someone said: What of the saying that injury should be repaid with kindness? The Master said: Then with what will you repay kindness? Repay injury with uprightness, and repay kindness with kindness.

The Master said: Alas, no one knows me! Tsze-kung said: What do you mean — no one knows you? The Master said: I make no complaint against Heaven, I lay no blame on men. My studies are of low and common things, and my understanding reaches to the heights. The one who knows me — is that not Heaven?

Kung-po Liao had slandered Tsze-lu to Chi-sun. Tsze-fu Ching-po brought word of it to Confucius, saying: My lord is certainly being led astray by Kung-po Liao, but I still have the power to have Liao cut down and his corpse displayed in the marketplace. The Master said: Whether my Way is to go forward, that is fate. Whether it is to come to nothing, that is fate. What can Kung-po Liao do against fate?
The Master said: Some men of worth withdraw from the world; some withdraw from a particular state; some withdraw at the first slighting look; some withdraw at the first word of insult.
The Master said: Those who did this were seven men.
Tsze-lu spent a night at Shih-man. The gatekeeper said: Where do you come from? Tsze-lu said: From the house of K'ung. The man said: Is that the one who knows it cannot be done and keeps on trying?

The Master was beating the stone chimes one day in Wei, when a man carrying a straw basket passed the door and said: There is a full heart in the way he strikes those chimes! After a while he added: How petty this stubborn clanging is! If no one takes any notice of you, then have done with it. "Where the water is deep, wade through clothes and all; where it is shallow, hold your skirts up and cross." The Master said: How firmly set he is — there is no answering that!

Tsze-chang said: What does the Book of History mean when it says that Kao-tsung, in the mourning hut, did not speak for three years? The Master said: Why single out Kao-tsung? All the ancients did the same. When the ruler died, the officers each kept to their posts and took their orders from the prime minister for three years.
The Master said: When those above love ritual, the people are easy to command.

Tsze-lu asked what makes a cultivated person. The Master said: He cultivates himself to become reverent and careful. Is that all? asked Tsze-lu. He cultivates himself so as to bring rest to others. Is that all? asked Tsze-lu. The Master said: He cultivates himself so as to bring rest to all the people. To cultivate yourself so as to bring rest to all the people — even Yao and Shun found that hard.

Yuan Zang sat sprawling on his heels, waiting for the Master, who said: As a boy, no respect for your elders; grown up, nothing worth handing down; and old now, and still not dead — you are a pest. And with that he rapped him on the shin with his staff.

A boy of the village of Ch'ueh was carrying messages for Confucius. Someone asked about him: Is he one who is making real progress? The Master said: I see him take the seat meant for a grown man, and walk shoulder to shoulder with his elders. He is not after progress; he wants to be a man before his time.

Duke Ling of Wei asked Confucius about battle formations. Confucius answered: I have learned about the vessels of sacrifice, but I have never studied warfare. The next day he left. In Ch'an the provisions ran out, and his followers grew so weak they could not get to their feet. Tsze-lu, plainly aggrieved, said: Must the cultivated person endure such want as this? The Master said: The cultivated person endures want and holds firm; the small man, in want, breaks loose into license.
The Master said: Ts'ze, you take me, I suppose, for one who learns many things and holds them all in mind? He answered: Yes — is that not so? No, said the Master: I thread it all on a single thread.
The Master said: Yu, how few are those who understand virtue.
The Master said: Was it not Shun who ruled by doing nothing? For what did he do? He composed himself in reverence and faced south, and that was all.

Tsze-chang asked how a man should carry himself to get on everywhere. The Master said: Let his words be faithful and true, his actions honest and careful, and he will get on even among the rude tribes of the south and north. Let his words be neither faithful nor true, his actions neither honest nor careful, and will he get on even in his own neighborhood? When you stand, see these words ranged before you; when you ride, see them resting on the yoke. Then you may carry them into practice. Tsze-chang wrote them on the end of his sash.

The Master said: Straight indeed was the recorder Yu! When the state had good government, he was an arrow; when it had bad government, he was an arrow still. A cultivated person indeed is Chu Po-yu! When the state had good government, he took office; when it had bad government, he could roll up his principles and keep them in his breast.

The Master said: When a man is worth speaking to, and you do not speak to him, you lose the man. When a man is not worth speaking to, and you speak to him, you waste your words. The wise lose neither the man nor their words.
The Master said: The scholar set on his purpose, and the humane man, will not seek life at the cost of their humaneness; there are times they will give their lives to keep their humaneness whole.

Tsze-kung asked about the practice of humaneness. The Master said: A workman who would do his work well must first sharpen his tools. Living in a state, take service under the worthiest of its ministers, and make friends of the most humane among its scholars.

Yen Yuan asked how a country should be governed. The Master said: Keep the seasons of the Hsia. Ride in the carriage of the Yin. Wear the cap of the Chau. For music, the Shao with its dances. Banish the tunes of Chang and keep glib talkers at a distance; the tunes of Chang are licentious, and glib talkers are dangerous.
The Master said: A man who gives no thought to what is far off will find his troubles close at hand.
The Master said: It is hopeless! I have yet to see a man who loved virtue as he loves a beautiful face.
The Master said: Did not Tsang Wan steal his post? He knew the worth of Hui of Liu-hsia, and yet would not stand him beside himself at court.
The Master said: Demand much of yourself, little of others, and you will keep resentment far off.
The Master said: A man who never asks himself, "How shall I handle this? How shall I handle this?" — with such a man there is nothing I can do.
The Master said: A whole day together, and not a word of their talk touches on what is right, while they delight in showing off small cleverness — there is no helping such men.

The Master said: The cultivated person takes what is right as the ground of all he does. He carries it out with ritual, brings it forth in humility, and completes it in good faith. That is the cultivated person.
The Master said: The cultivated person is distressed by his own incapacity; he is not distressed that others fail to know him.
The Master said: The cultivated person hates the thought of leaving the world with his name unspoken.
The Master said: The cultivated person seeks it in himself; the small man seeks it in others.
The Master said: The cultivated person has self-respect and does not quarrel; he keeps company with others and joins no faction.
The Master said: The cultivated person does not raise a man up for his words alone, nor throw out good words because of the man who speaks them.
Tsze-kung asked: Is there a single word one can practice all one's life? The Master said: Is it not reciprocity? What you do not want done to yourself, do not do to others.

The Master said: In my dealings with men, whose evil have I blamed, whose good have I praised, beyond what was deserved? If I have praised any beyond their due, there was ground for it once I had looked into the man. This is the people through whom the three dynasties held to their straight course.
The Master said: Even in my own day a recorder would leave a blank where he was unsure, and a man with a horse would lend it to another to ride. Now even that is gone.
The Master said: Clever words confound virtue; a little impatience confounds great plans.
The Master said: When the many hate a man, look into it for yourself; when the many love a man, look into it for yourself.
The Master said: A man can enlarge the Way; the Way does not enlarge the man.
The Master said: To err and not mend it — that is to err indeed.
The Master said: Once I went a whole day without food and a whole night without sleep, given over to thought. It came to nothing. Better to learn.

The Master said: The cultivated person sets his mind on the Way, not on his food. Take to farming, and hunger may still find you; take to learning, and a salary may follow. The cultivated person worries about the Way, not about poverty.

The Master said: Knowledge enough to reach it, but not virtue enough to hold it — what you gain, you will lose again. Knowledge enough to reach it, virtue enough to hold it, but no dignity in governing — and the people will not respect you. Knowledge enough to reach it, virtue enough to hold it, dignity in governing — but if you set the people moving against ritual, it is still not good enough.
The Master said: The cultivated person cannot be known in small things, but may be entrusted with great ones; the small man cannot be entrusted with great things, but may be known in small ones.
The Master said: Humaneness is more to the people than water and fire. I have seen men die from treading on water and fire; I have never seen a man die from treading the path of humaneness.
The Master said: Where humaneness is at stake, give way to no one, not even your teacher.
The Master said: The cultivated person is firm where it is right, not stubborn for its own sake.
The Master said: In serving his ruler, a man should attend to his duties first and put his pay second.
The Master said: In teaching there are no classes of men.
The Master said: Those who walk by different ways cannot lay plans together.
The Master said: In speech, all that is asked is that it carry the meaning.

The music-master Mien came to call. When they reached the steps, the Master said: Here are the steps. When they reached the mat, he said: Here is the mat. When all were seated, he told him: So-and-so is here, so-and-so is there. After the music-master Mien had gone, Tsze-chang asked: Is that the way to speak with a music-master? The Master said: Yes. That is certainly the way to help the blind.
